title: Old Testament Survey: God's Promise Unfolding
description: Journey through the entire Old Testament, creation and the patriarchs, the exodus and the Law, the kings and prophets, exile and return, and see how it all points to Christ.

lessons.title: 1.1 The Old Testament: One Story in 39 Books
lessons.html:
The Old Testament: One Story in 39 Books

The Old Testament is the first and larger part of the Bible, 39 books written over roughly a thousand years, in Hebrew (with a little Aramaic). Though it contains history, law, poetry, and prophecy, it tells one unfolding story: how the one true God created the world, chose a people, and prepared the way for a Savior.

How the Old Testament is arranged

  • The Law (Torah / Pentateuch), Genesis to Deuteronomy: creation, the patriarchs, the exodus, and God's covenant law.
  • History, Joshua to Esther: Israel in the Promised Land, the kings, exile, and return.
  • Poetry & Wisdom, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs.
  • Prophets, Isaiah to Malachi: God's messengers calling His people back and pointing to the future.

Jesus Himself said the whole Old Testament points to Him: the Scriptures "bear witness about me" (John 5:39), and He explained "in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27). So we do not read the Old Testament as a museum of old stories, but as the first act of the drama that reaches its climax in Christ.

As you begin this survey, keep asking three questions of every passage: What does this reveal about God? What does it show about people and sin? How does it move the story toward the promised Savior? These questions turn ancient text into living truth.

lessons.title: 1.2 Genesis: Creation, Fall, and Promise
lessons.html:
Genesis: Creation, Fall, and Promise

Genesis means "beginnings," and it explains where everything comes from. It opens with the majestic account of God creating the heavens and the earth and forming humanity in His image (Genesis 1:27), placing them in a good world with meaningful work and relationship with Him.

The Fall

In Genesis 3, the first humans disobeyed God, and sin entered the world, bringing shame, broken relationships, hardship, and death. Yet even in judgment God gave hope: He promised that a descendant of the woman would one day crush the serpent (Genesis 3:15). Christians call this the "first gospel," the first hint of the Savior to come.

From bad to worse, and a rescue

Sin spread quickly: Cain murdered Abel, and the world grew so corrupt that God sent a flood, saving Noah and his family (Genesis 6-9). At Babel, human pride scattered the nations (Genesis 11). The pattern is clear: humanity keeps failing, but God keeps pursuing.

Genesis lays the foundation for the entire Bible. Every major theme begins here, God as Creator, humanity's dignity and fall, sin's spread, judgment, grace, and the promise of redemption. When you understand Genesis 1-11, you understand the "problem" that the rest of Scripture answers.

lessons.title: 1.3 The Patriarchs & The Exodus
lessons.html:
The Patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob

Beginning in Genesis 12, God narrows His focus to one man through whom He will bless the whole world. He called Abraham out of his homeland with an astonishing promise: "I will make of you a great nation... and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed" (Genesis 12:2-3). This is God's covenant, a binding promise that shapes the rest of the Bible.

A faith that trusted God

Abraham believed God's promise even when it seemed impossible, he and Sarah were old and childless. "He believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6), a verse the New Testament quotes to explain salvation by faith. God tested Abraham's faith on Mount Moriah, then provided a substitute sacrifice (Genesis 22), a powerful foreshadowing of the cross.

Isaac, Jacob, and the twelve tribes

The promise passed to Abraham's son Isaac, then to Jacob (renamed Israel), whose twelve sons became the twelve tribes of Israel. Jacob's son Joseph was sold into slavery in Egypt by his brothers, yet God raised him to power to save many lives during famine. Joseph's words capture a key Bible theme: "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20).

The patriarchs were flawed people, yet God worked through them faithfully. Their story shows that God's promises depend on His faithfulness, not human perfection, a comfort to every believer.

lessons.title: 2.1 Exodus: Rescue, Passover, and the Law
lessons.html:
Exodus: Rescue, Passover, and the Law

Generations after Joseph, the Israelites had multiplied in Egypt but were enslaved by a cruel Pharaoh. The book of Exodus tells how God heard their cry and raised up Moses to lead them out (Exodus 3). This great rescue, the exodus, became the defining event of Israel's history and a picture of salvation itself.

The Passover

After nine plagues, God sent a final judgment, but spared every home that placed the blood of a lamb on its doorposts. This Passover (Exodus 12) rescued Israel and pointed forward to Jesus, "our Passover lamb" (1 Corinthians 5:7), whose blood saves us from judgment. God then parted the Red Sea, delivering His people and defeating Pharaoh's army.

The Law at Sinai

At Mount Sinai, God gave Israel His Law, including the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20). The Law revealed God's holy character and how His covenant people should live, loving God and loving neighbor. It was never meant to earn salvation (God had already rescued them by grace) but to shape a redeemed people and expose sin.

God also instructed Israel to build the tabernacle, a portable tent where His presence would dwell among them. The exodus teaches a pattern the whole Bible follows: God rescues His people by grace, then calls them to live as His own.

lessons.title: 2.2 Wilderness and the Edge of the Promised Land
lessons.html:
Wilderness and the Edge of the Promised Land

After Sinai, Israel journeyed toward the land God had promised. The books of Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy cover this wilderness period, teaching Israel how to worship a holy God and live as His covenant people.

Leviticus: how sinful people approach a holy God

Leviticus lays out the sacrifices and priesthood that allowed a sinful people to live near a holy God. Again and again, sin required a substitute; "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness" (Hebrews 9:22). These sacrifices pointed forward to the perfect sacrifice of Christ. The command "be holy, for I am holy" (Leviticus 19:2) runs through the book.

Numbers: failure and faithfulness

At the border of the Promised Land, Israel refused to trust God and believed the report that the land could not be taken. Because of this unbelief, that generation wandered forty years in the wilderness (Numbers 14). Yet God faithfully provided manna, water, and guidance the entire time.

Deuteronomy: remember and obey

Before entering the land, Moses gave farewell sermons urging the new generation to love and obey God: "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart" (Deuteronomy 6:4-5), the verse Jesus called the greatest commandment. The wilderness years teach that unbelief forfeits blessing, but God's faithfulness never fails.

lessons.title: 2.3 Conquest and the Judges
lessons.html:
Conquest and the Judges

After Moses died, Joshua led Israel into the Promised Land of Canaan. God gave clear encouragement: "Be strong and courageous... for the Lord your God is with you wherever you go" (Joshua 1:9). Through miraculous victories, beginning with the walls of Jericho (Joshua 6), Israel took possession of the land God had promised to Abraham centuries earlier.

A troubling cycle

The book of Judges describes what happened next, and it is sobering. Israel repeatedly fell into a cycle: the people sinned and served other gods, God allowed oppression by enemies, the people cried out, and God raised up a deliverer (a "judge") to rescue them, until they sinned again. Leaders like Deborah, Gideon, and Samson appear in this period.

The book's tragic refrain explains the chaos: "In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25). Without godly leadership and faithfulness to the covenant, the nation drifted into moral confusion.

The era of the judges reveals a deep human need: people cannot save themselves by their own goodness, and they long for a true and righteous king. That longing sets the stage for the monarchy, and ultimately for the King of kings, Jesus.

lessons.title: 3.1 Job and the Question of Suffering
lessons.html:
Job and the Question of Suffering

The Old Testament does not avoid life's hardest questions. The book of Job wrestles honestly with suffering: why do good people suffer? Job was "blameless and upright" (Job 1:1), yet he lost his children, wealth, and health in a series of disasters.

Wrong answers and honest questions

Job's friends insisted his suffering must be punishment for secret sin, a simple but false explanation. Job refused to curse God, but he questioned deeply and demanded answers. The book gives us permission to bring our pain and confusion honestly to God rather than pretending everything is fine.

God's answer

When God finally spoke, He did not explain why. Instead He revealed His own greatness and wisdom as Creator (Job 38-41), reminding Job that God's ways are higher than ours. Job responded in humble trust: "I know that you can do all things" (Job 42:2). In the end God restored Job.

Job teaches that suffering is not always punishment, that God is trustworthy even when we cannot understand, and that faith can hold on in the dark. For Christians, Job also points ahead: our questions find their deepest answer at the cross, where the truly blameless One suffered for us and rose in victory.

lessons.title: 3.2 The Psalms: Prayers and Songs
lessons.html:
The Psalms: Prayers and Songs for Every Season

The book of Psalms is the Bible's songbook and prayer book, 150 poems expressing the full range of human emotion before God: joy, sorrow, fear, anger, gratitude, and hope. For thousands of years believers have found their own hearts put into words here.

Types of psalms

  • Praise, celebrating who God is and what He has done (Psalm 100).
  • Lament, honest cries in suffering that still turn toward trust (Psalm 13).
  • Thanksgiving, gratitude for God's rescue and provision (Psalm 30).
  • Trust, resting in God's care, like the beloved "The Lord is my shepherd" (Psalm 23).
  • Messianic, pointing to the coming Christ, such as Psalm 22, which describes the crucifixion centuries before it happened.

Many psalms were written by King David, "a man after God's own heart" (1 Samuel 13:14). They teach us that God welcomes honesty, we can bring Him our fear and even our complaints, and that worship is meant to be woven through all of life.

The Psalms model a healthy prayer life: they praise God for who He is, remember His past faithfulness, pour out present troubles, and choose to trust Him for the future. Praying the Psalms is one of the best ways to grow in prayer.

lessons.title: 3.3 Proverbs and the Wisdom Books
lessons.html:
Proverbs and the Wisdom Books

The wisdom books, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Songs, teach how to live skillfully in God's world. If the Law tells us God's commands and the Psalms give us God's songs, the wisdom books give us God's practical guidance for everyday decisions.

Proverbs: skill for living

Proverbs is a collection of short, memorable sayings about work, money, speech, friendship, family, and self-control. Its foundational principle is this: "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge" (Proverbs 1:7). To "fear the Lord" means to reverence Him, and that reverence is where real wisdom starts. Proverbs urges us to trust God rather than our own understanding (Proverbs 3:5-6).

Ecclesiastes: life "under the sun"

Ecclesiastes honestly explores how empty life feels when we chase pleasure, wealth, or success apart from God, "vanity of vanities" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). Its conclusion is to "fear God and keep his commandments" (Ecclesiastes 12:13), for lasting meaning is found only in Him.

These books remind us that faith is meant to be lived out in practical, daily ways, in how we speak, spend, work, and relate to others. True wisdom is not merely being clever; it is living God's way in God's world, and it begins with reverence for Him.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Project: A Psalm of Your Own
lessons.html: Module 3 Project, A Psalm of Your Own. Using the Psalms as your model, write a short prayer-poem (8–16 lines) to God about something real in your life right now, a joy to thank Him for, a fear to bring Him, or a struggle to lay before Him. Follow the pattern many psalms use: begin by honestly naming your situation, then remember something true about God, and end by choosing to trust Him. Include at least one truth you learned from Job, Psalms, or Proverbs. This exercise turns the wisdom books into personal worship.

lessons.title: 4.1 The Kings: David, Solomon, and a Divided Nation
lessons.html:
The Kings: David, Solomon, and a Divided Nation

Israel's longing for a king was answered first with Saul, who began well but disobeyed God and was rejected. Then God chose David, a shepherd boy who trusted God enough to face the giant Goliath (1 Samuel 17). Though imperfect, his sin with Bathsheba was grievous, David was "a man after God's own heart" who repented deeply (Psalm 51).

God's covenant with David

God made a stunning promise to David: one of his descendants would reign on his throne forever (2 Samuel 7:12-16). This "Davidic covenant" pointed beyond any earthly king to the eternal King, Jesus, "the son of David" (Matthew 1:1).

Solomon and the split

David's son Solomon built the magnificent temple in Jerusalem and became famous for his wisdom, but late in life his many foreign wives turned his heart to idols. After Solomon, the kingdom split in two: Israel in the north (ten tribes) and Judah in the south (1 Kings 12).

From then on, most kings led the people into idolatry, though a few, like Hezekiah and Josiah, brought reform. The story of the kings shows that even the best human rulers fail, deepening the Bible's longing for the perfect King who alone can rule in righteousness forever.

lessons.title: 4.2 The Major Prophets
lessons.html:
The Major Prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel

As Israel and Judah drifted into idolatry and injustice, God sent prophets, His messengers who called the people back to the covenant, warned of coming judgment, and promised future hope. The "Major Prophets" are named for the length of their books, not their importance.

Isaiah, the gospel prophet

Isaiah announced judgment but also breathtaking hope, including some of the clearest prophecies of the Messiah. He foretold a child born to reign (Isaiah 9:6) and a "suffering servant" who "was pierced for our transgressions" and by "his wounds we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5), written centuries before Jesus.

Jeremiah and Ezekiel

Jeremiah, the "weeping prophet," warned Judah of the Babylonian exile yet promised a coming "new covenant" written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31-33). Ezekiel, prophesying among the exiles, saw visions of God's glory and promised God would give His people "a new heart" and put His Spirit within them (Ezekiel 36:26-27).

Daniel, faithful in a foreign land

Daniel remained faithful to God in the Babylonian empire, famously in the lions' den (Daniel 6), and received visions of God's eternal kingdom that "shall never be destroyed" (Daniel 2:44). The prophets prove God is sovereign over history and always keeps His word.

lessons.title: 4.3 The Minor Prophets
lessons.html:
The Minor Prophets: Twelve Voices, One Message

The twelve "Minor Prophets", from Hosea to Malachi, are shorter books, but their messages are powerful. Though written to specific situations, they share common themes: God hates sin and injustice, He calls His people to repent, judgment is real, and mercy is always offered to those who return.

A few memorable messages

  • Hosea, through his own painful marriage, pictures God's faithful love for an unfaithful people.
  • Joel, calls for repentance and promises God will pour out His Spirit (Joel 2:28), fulfilled at Pentecost.
  • Amos, thunders against injustice: "let justice roll down like waters" (Amos 5:24).
  • Jonah, shows God's mercy reaching even Israel's enemies in Nineveh.
  • Micah, foretold the Messiah's birthplace, Bethlehem (Micah 5:2), and summarized true religion: "do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God" (Micah 6:8).
  • Malachi, the last Old Testament book, promises a messenger will prepare the way for the Lord (Malachi 3:1).

Together the prophets do two things at once: they hold up a mirror to show the people their sin, and they open a window to show a future hope, a coming King, a new covenant, and God's Spirit poured out. After Malachi came 400 years of silence, until the promised messenger, John the Baptist, announced the arrival of Jesus.

lessons.title: 5.1 Exile: When the Nation Fell
lessons.html:
Exile: When the Nation Fell

The prophets' warnings came true. Because of persistent idolatry and injustice, God allowed His people to be conquered and carried away. The northern kingdom of Israel fell to Assyria in 722 BC, and the southern kingdom of Judah fell to Babylon, which destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 586 BC and took the people into exile.

Loss and lament

The exile was a national catastrophe: the temple destroyed, the land lost, the people scattered. The book of Lamentations pours out grief over the fallen city. Yet even here, hope shines: "The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases; his mercies... are new every morning" (Lamentations 3:22-23).

God with His people in a foreign land

Even in Babylon, God did not abandon His people. Through Jeremiah He told the exiles to settle down, "seek the welfare of the city" where they lived, and pray for it (Jeremiah 29:7), then gave the famous promise, "For I know the plans I have for you... plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). Daniel and his friends showed that one can remain faithful to God even under a pagan empire.

The exile taught Israel painful but vital lessons: sin has serious consequences, idols are worthless, and yet God remains faithful to His covenant. He had promised judgment for unfaithfulness, but He had also promised to bring His people home.

lessons.title: 5.2 Return and Rebuilding: Ezra, Nehemiah
lessons.html:
Return and Rebuilding: Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai

God kept His promise to restore His people. After about seventy years, the Persian empire conquered Babylon, and King Cyrus allowed the Jews to return home (Ezra 1), just as the prophets had foretold. The books of Ezra and Nehemiah tell the story of this return and rebuilding.

Rebuilding the temple and the walls

Under leaders like Zerubbabel and the encouragement of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, the returned exiles rebuilt the temple, though it was humbler than Solomon's (Ezra 3). Decades later, Nehemiah, a cupbearer to the Persian king, returned to rebuild Jerusalem's broken walls, finishing the work in just 52 days despite fierce opposition (Nehemiah 6:15). His prayerful, courageous leadership is a model for God's people facing hard tasks.

Renewing the covenant

Ezra, a scribe and teacher, led a spiritual renewal by reading and explaining God's Law to the people, who wept and then rejoiced as they understood it (Nehemiah 8). This restored community recommitted to following God.

The return shows God's unfailing faithfulness: He disciplines His people, but He does not abandon them. He brought them home to keep His larger promise alive, for from this restored people would one day come the Messiah.

lessons.title: 5.3 Esther and the Hidden Hand of God
lessons.html:
Esther and the Hidden Hand of God

Not all the exiles returned home; many remained scattered across the Persian empire. The book of Esther is set among these Jews and tells a dramatic story of deliverance, remarkable because God is never once mentioned by name, yet His providence is visible on every page.

The story

A young Jewish woman named Esther became queen of Persia, hiding her identity. When a powerful official named Haman plotted to destroy all the Jews, Esther's cousin Mordecai urged her to act, with words that ring through history: "Who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esther 4:14).

At great personal risk, Esther approached the king to plead for her people. Through a series of "coincidences", a sleepless king, a timely record read aloud, a reversal of fortunes, Haman's plot collapsed, and the Jews were saved. The festival of Purim still celebrates this deliverance.

The lesson: God works even when unseen

Esther teaches one of the Bible's most comforting truths: God is at work even when He seems silent or invisible. There are no dramatic miracles here, just ordinary events that, woven together, accomplish God's saving purpose. When your life feels like God is far away, Esther reminds you that His hidden hand is guiding history, and He can place you exactly where you are needed "for such a time as this."

modules.title: Module 6: Themes & Christ in the OT

lessons.title: 6.1 The Covenants: God's Unfolding Plan
lessons.html:
The Covenants: God's Unfolding Plan

To read the Old Testament well, you need to understand covenants, the binding promises through which God relates to His people. Like threads in a rope, these covenants tie the whole story together and lead directly to Jesus.

The major covenants

  • With Noah, God promised never again to destroy the earth by flood, sealing it with the rainbow (Genesis 9).
  • With Abraham, God promised land, descendants, and blessing to all nations through him (Genesis 12, 15, 17).
  • With Moses (Israel), God gave the Law at Sinai, forming Israel as His covenant nation (Exodus 19-24).
  • With David, God promised an everlasting throne through David's line (2 Samuel 7).
  • The New Covenant, promised through Jeremiah, God would forgive sins and write His law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31-34), fulfilled by Jesus.

Each covenant advances one great plan: God is redeeming a people for Himself and, through them, blessing the whole world. The promises to Abraham and David find their "Yes" in Christ, "For all the promises of God find their Yes in him" (2 Corinthians 1:20).

Understanding the covenants keeps the Old Testament from feeling like scattered stories. It is one connected drama of a faithful God keeping His word across the centuries, until the promised Savior finally arrives.

lessons.title: 6.2 Christ in the Old Testament
lessons.html:
Christ in the Old Testament

Jesus taught that the entire Old Testament is about Him (Luke 24:27, 44). Once you know what to look for, you will see the coming Savior foreshadowed everywhere, in promises, pictures, and prophecies.

Prophecies fulfilled in Jesus

  • Born of a virgin (Isaiah 7:14) in Bethlehem (Micah 5:2).
  • A descendant of Abraham and David (Genesis 12:3; 2 Samuel 7).
  • The suffering servant "pierced for our transgressions" (Isaiah 53).
  • His crucifixion pictured in detail (Psalm 22), written long before crucifixion was practiced.

Pictures and patterns

Beyond direct prophecy, the Old Testament is full of "types", persons and events that foreshadow Christ. The Passover lamb whose blood saves (Exodus 12); the sacrificial system that pointed to a final sacrifice; the bronze serpent lifted up to heal (Numbers 21), which Jesus applied to Himself (John 3:14); and priests, kings, and prophets who all anticipated the one who is Prophet, Priest, and King.

This is why the Old Testament matters so much for Christians. It is not merely background; it is the God-designed preparation for the gospel. The more you understand the promises, the sacrifices, and the longing for a King, the more amazing the arrival of Jesus becomes, the fulfillment of everything God had been promising for centuries.

lessons.title: 6.3 Reading the Old Testament Today
lessons.html:
Reading the Old Testament Today

You have surveyed the whole Old Testament, from creation to the return from exile, through law, history, poetry, and prophecy. This final lesson helps you keep reading it wisely and fruitfully for the rest of your life.

Four practical guidelines

  1. Read it as one story that leads to Jesus. Always ask how a passage fits into God's big plan of redemption fulfilled in Christ.
  2. Learn about God's character. Every book reveals His holiness, justice, patience, and steadfast love. The God of the Old Testament is the same God we worship today.
  3. Apply timeless truths, not every ancient command directly. The moral truths (love God, do justice, care for the poor) still apply; the ceremonial laws pointed to Christ and are fulfilled in Him.
  4. Let it shape your prayer and worship. Pray the Psalms, learn from the failures of the kings, and take courage from God's faithfulness across the generations.

The Old Testament is not obsolete. Paul wrote that "whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that... we might have hope" (Romans 15:4). Its stories warn us, its promises encourage us, and its whole message prepares us to treasure Jesus.

Consider continuing with the New Testament Survey course to see how every Old Testament promise is fulfilled in Christ and His Church. Keep reading, God's Word will feed your soul for a lifetime.

questions.explanation: The 39 books tell one story of God preparing the way for Christ.

questions.explanation: Genesis 1-3 covers creation and the Fall.

options: All the families of the earth
questions.explanation: Genesis 12:3, through Abraham all nations would be blessed.

questions.question: The Passover pointed forward to:
questions.explanation: The Passover lamb foreshadowed Christ, our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).

questions.question: Joshua is known for leading Israel to:
questions.explanation: Joshua led the conquest of Canaan.

questions.question: "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge" is the theme of:

questions.question: Job wrestles honestly with the question of:

questions.question: God promised David that his descendant would:
questions.explanation: 2 Samuel 7 promises an everlasting throne, fulfilled in Jesus.

questions.explanation: The kingdom divided into north (Israel) and south (Judah).

questions.question: Isaiah 53 famously describes:
questions.explanation: Isaiah 53 foretells the Messiah as the suffering servant.

questions.question: Jeremiah promised a "new covenant" that would be:
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 31:31-33 promises the law written on the heart.

questions.question: Judah was taken into exile by Babylon because of:
questions.explanation: Exile came as judgment for ongoing unfaithfulness, as the prophets warned.

questions.question: Nehemiah is remembered for rebuilding:
questions.explanation: Nehemiah led the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls.

questions.question: The book of Esther highlights God's:

questions.question: The covenants of the Bible find their "Yes" in:
questions.explanation: All God's promises are fulfilled in Jesus.

questions.question: Jesus taught that the Old Testament Scriptures:
questions.explanation: Jesus said the Scriptures testify about Him (John 5:39; Luke 24:27).

questions.question: A good way to read the Old Testament today is to:
options: Read it as one story leading to Jesus
questions.explanation: Read the OT as God's unified story of redemption fulfilled in Christ.
